nameStory: The Small Yellow Onion gets its straightforward name from its bright yellow flowers and compact size compared to other wild onions. The scientific name 'flavum' comes from the Latin word for yellow, making this one of the easier plant names to remember!
description: Small Yellow Onion is a petite bulbous perennial that produces clusters of cheerful bright yellow flowers atop slender stems. Growing from an underground bulb like its garden relatives, this Mediterranean native typically reaches 8-12 inches tall. The plant has narrow, grass-like leaves and that unmistakable oniony smell when crushed. It's extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers arranged in loose, rounded clusters (umbels) at the top of naked stems, each tiny flower star-shaped with 6 petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the base, bluish-green in color and hollow when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Strong oniony smell when any part of the plant is bruised or crushed, similar to chives or green onions

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing clumps with flower stems rising 8-12 inches above the foliage, growing from small underground bulbs

habitat: As a Mediterranean native, Small Yellow Onion would likely be found in well-drained, sunny locations such as rock gardens, disturbed soils, or areas around old homesites where it might have escaped cultivation. Given its extreme rarity in New England, any sighting would most likely be near human habitation rather than in wild natural areas.

seasonality.spring: New grass-like leaves emerge from bulbs as soil warms, forming small clumps of bluish-green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flower clusters bloom on slender stems, creating the plant's most distinctive and identifiable feature.
seasonality.fall: Foliage begins to yellow and die back as the plant prepares to go dormant, with energy returning to the underground bulb.
seasonality.winter: Plant is completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, surviving as a small bulb underground.

funFact: Despite being called 'small,' this little onion relative can produce bulbs that are actually quite flavorful and edible, traditionally used in Mediterranean cooking much like shallots or pearl onions!
confusionNotes: With bright yellow flowers, Small Yellow Onion is actually quite distinct from most other wild onions in New England, which typically have white, pink, or purple blooms. The yellow flowers combined with the onion scent make this nearly unmistakable, though you might initially mistake the foliage for grass until you smell it.
contextualKnowledge: This species is native to regions around the Mediterranean, Black, and Caspian Seas, making it a true exotic in New England. Its presence here would almost certainly indicate garden escape or intentional planting rather than natural occurrence.
compareHints: Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers. The closest relative in terms of flower color might be Yellow Onion (Allium moly), but that species has broader leaves and different flower structure.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.
Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms.
Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
